content: After one year of disseminating the guidelines, a needs evaluation survey will be conducted. The survey results will help identify challenges and barriers to the adoption of the guidelines, assess their effectiveness in improving sexually transmitted infection (STI) service delivery, and highlight topics or gaps in STI management that require attention in future updates. The guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations for managing symptomatic STIs, primarily using a syndromic approach. This approach is particularly beneficial for resource-limited settings, enabling the delivery of effective interventions. The guidelines address common syndromes such as urethral discharge in men, vaginal discharge and pelvic inflammatory disease in women, genital ulcers in both sexes, and anorectal infections. However, the epidemiology of the pathogens causing these syndromes varies geographically, necessitating local data to tailor interventions. Additionally, monitoring antimicrobial resistance patterns is critical, as it may require adjustments in the choice of medications for each syndrome. In the absence of local data, the globally assessed recommendations in the guidelines can be adopted as they are. Opportunities for integrated approaches include expanding rapid point-of-care testing for STIs, leveraging existing facilities for HIV testing, and scaling up dual or triple elimination projects that test for HIV, syphilis, and viral hepatitis simultaneously. Molecular testing technologies, already used for tuberculosis and viral load detection, can be expanded to sentinel sites or designated laboratories to diagnose STIs, identify the causes of syndromes, and detect antimicrobial resistance markers in pathogens like Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Mycoplasma genitalium as technologies become more accessible and affordable. Healthcare providers should receive integrated training to implement the guidelines effectively, enhancing services for HIV, STIs, antenatal care, and family planning. Countries should establish or strengthen referral centers and sentinel site laboratories to support primary healthcare services requiring specialist input, such as STI experts or gynecologists. These centers can also support STI programs by conducting etiological studies and monitoring antimicrobial resistance. In June 2020, a think-tank meeting of experts convened by the Department of Global HIV, Hepatitis, and STI Programs emphasized the importance of STI surveillance in global public health. Surveillance is essential for understanding the burden of STIs and informing effective interventions. Challenges in STI surveillance include limited laboratory testing, the asymptomatic nature of many STIs, and insufficient integration of laboratory and epidemiological data. Strengthening ongoing surveillance at the country level is crucial, using existing data as a foundation for improvement. Regular etiological studies using molecular assays should be conducted at sentinel sites to monitor the causes of STI syndromes and antimicrobial resistance. STI surveillance should be integrated into the syndromic approach and linked with periodic assessments of antimicrobial resistance in key pathogens. Monitoring STI complications and incorporating this data into management reporting systems is also essential. Surveillance in key populations, such as men who have sex with men and sex workers, remains fundamental, as these groups significantly contribute to the STI epidemic. Collaboration with NGOs can enhance data collection and intervention planning. Regular, systematic surveillance and screening in these populations are more effective than occasional efforts. Capacity-building for STI surveillance requires investment in laboratory infrastructure, human resources, and access to affordable diagnostic tests. Advocacy for funding is essential to develop alternative approaches for managing STIs, including rapid point-of-care diagnostic tests. For syphilis, routine maternal screening and trend estimation should be scaled up using modeling tools to estimate maternal and congenital syphilis trends. Research is needed to address outstanding questions in STI case management, such as the role of overtreatment in antimicrobial resistance and the pathogenicity of organisms like Mycoplasma genitalium. Studies should also focus on the resurgence of lymphogranuloma venereum, particularly among men who have sex with men, and the long-term consequences of untreated infections. Validation and cost-effectiveness studies of recommended flowcharts, as well as research on anorectal and pharyngeal infections, are necessary. Developing affordable, rapid point-of-care tests for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis remains a priority.
